headline: Are Blood Glucose Meters Accurate? FDA Standards, Common Errors, and Tips for Trustworthy Readings
description: Wondering are blood glucose meters accurate? Learn FDA accuracy standards, common user errors, and tips for reliable readings to support your diabetes management.

mainEntity.name: What is the acceptable error margin for home blood glucose meters?

acceptedAnswer.text: The FDA requires 95% of home glucose meter readings fall within ±15% of lab reference results, and 99% fall within ±20%. Readings within this range are considered clinically accurate and will not impact standard diabetes treatment decisions.

mainEntity.name: Why do I get two different readings from the same meter minutes apart?

acceptedAnswer.text: Minor fluctuations of 10-15% are normal due to natural blood glucose changes, small user error, or acceptable device variance. If readings differ by more than 20%, run a control solution test to check your meter and strips for issues.

mainEntity.name: Do expired test strips make my glucose meter less accurate?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, expired test strips have degraded chemical coatings that can produce readings 20-30% higher or lower than actual levels. Discard strips 3 months after opening their vial, even if the printed expiration date is not yet passed.

mainEntity.name: How can I check if my blood glucose meter is working correctly?

acceptedAnswer.text: Use FDA-approved control solution matched to your meter and strip brand to run a test. If results fall outside the range printed on your test strip vial, clean your meter, use fresh strips, and retest. Contact the manufacturer if results remain out of range.

mainEntity.name: When should I replace my home blood glucose meter?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most glucose meters have a 3-5 year lifespan per manufacturer guidelines. Replace yours sooner if it sustains water damage, consistently produces out-of-range control test results, or fails to hold a charge or sync with your diabetes management tools.
